description: #5057 — the trash-lifecycle batch trio (`delete_blocks_by_ids`, `restore_blocks_by_ids`, `purge_blocks_by_ids`) driven through the command leg. What separates these from their single-block siblings is the COHORT: each acts on and reports every block the cascade reached, not the ids the caller listed. The fixture drives a delete that cascades DOWN a 3-level subtree, a restore that must bring back that exact cohort, a restore that must walk UP a tombstoned ancestor chain, a purge that must cascade to descendants while appending one op per ROOT, and every refusal the three share.
name: batch_trash_lifecycle

ops.comment: Two roots, one carrying a 2-level subtree. `deleted_count` is the whole cohort (S2+S3+S4, plus S5), not the two ids listed — that difference is the entire point of the batch variant.
ops.name: delete_alpha_and_beta

ops.comment: A page root, so `affected_page_ids` is non-empty. Its child rides the cascade without being listed, and is a content block so it does not join that list.
ops.name: delete_nested_page

ops.comment: S5 is already soft-deleted, so it is not in the cohort and not counted; only S8's cohort is. A skipped id is absent from `affected_page_ids` too.
ops.name: delete_skips_an_already_deleted_id

ops.comment: Restoring the ROOT alone must bring back S3 and S4 with it — the exact cohort the delete tombstoned — and unlike the ancestors in the next op, a cohort member IS counted. A handler that only clears `deleted_at` on the listed id answers 1 here instead of 3.
ops.name: restore_alpha_brings_back_its_cohort

ops.comment: S9's parent S8 is still tombstoned, so restoring S9 alone would leave a live block under a dead parent. The restore revives the ancestor chain too — S8 is live in the settled snapshot — while `affected_count` stays 1. Count and effect deliberately disagree here: the number reports the requested roots' cohort, not the ancestors dragged back with it. The op above pins the other half of that rule, where the cohort IS counted.
ops.name: restore_walks_up_the_tombstoned_ancestor_chain

ops.comment: S2 is live by now, restored two ops above. The restore path REFUSES a live id rather than filtering it out, which is the asymmetry worth pinning: a MISSING id is skipped on this same call, so "ignore what you cannot restore" is not the rule. Matches the single-block `restore_block`.
ops.name: restore_refuses_a_live_block

ops.comment: One root listed, two rows destroyed: the physical cascade reaches S7. `affected_count` counts rows, while the op log records one `purge_block` per ROOT — the two numbers are deliberately different and both are pinned here.
ops.name: purge_nested_page_cascades_to_descendants

ops.comment: A purge is the one destructive write that still records itself, so the op-log digest moves. A handler that purges silently leaves the digest behind.
ops.name: purge_beta_appends_an_op

ops.comment: Re-tombstones S8 and its child S9 so the op below can list BOTH as roots.
ops.name: delete_gamma_again_for_the_overlap_arm

ops.comment: S9 sits inside S8's delete cohort, so restoring S8 revives S9 on the way. Both are still ROOTS the caller named: the op log carries one `restore_block` per resolved root, not one per row that was still tombstoned by the time its turn came. A handler that re-reads `deleted_at` in a second pass skips S9 and appends one op where the backend appends two — visible only in the digest, since the settled state is identical either way.
ops.name: restore_counts_one_op_per_root_even_when_they_overlap

ops.comment: S1 is live. The batch path refuses rather than silently skipping, because its physical cascade is seeded from the raw input list: hard-deleting a live subtree with no op is unsynced data loss no peer ever hears about (#3819).
ops.name: purge_refuses_a_live_block

ops.comment: An empty batch is a caller bug, not a no-op.
ops.name: purge_refuses_an_empty_list

ops.comment: The same guard on the restore path.
ops.name: restore_refuses_an_empty_list

ops.comment: The same guard on the delete path.
ops.name: delete_refuses_an_empty_list
